newsitem.title: UK: BADMINTON-RASMUSSEN TAKES WORLD CROWN AFTER 125-MINUTE EPIC.
newsitem.headline: BADMINTON-RASMUSSEN TAKES WORLD CROWN AFTER 125-MINUTE EPIC.

text.p: Peter Rasmussen captured the world badminton title on Sunday in one of the most dramatic games the sport has seen.
Rasmussen overcame gallant Chinese Sun Jun 16-17 18-13 15-10 in a 125-minute epic -- a world championship record.
Sun led 5-3 and 10-3 in the deciding game only to suffer two serious attacks of cramp.
The Chinese soldiered on, heavily bandaged, but Rasmussen, seeded only 15, levelled at 10-10 and went on to claim Denmark's first men's singles crown for 20 years.

Rasmussen is the new kid on the block in Danish badminton, ranked behind such as Olympic champion Poul-Erik Hoyer-Larsen, but the battling qualities shown on Sunday augur strongly he will be around for some time to come.
It looked in the second game as if the title was heading to China as Sun reeled off seven successive points to lead 13-6 with the crown just two tantalising points away.
But Rasmussen, all heart and big, accurate smashing, clawed back to 13-13 and then 18-13 to capture the game.
The Dane led 3-0 in the decider only for Sun, seeded three, to find fresh heart in the sweltering conditions of the indoor leisure centre and go clear at 5-3.

Both men had come through tough semifinals on Saturday -- Sun in a 82-minute clash with Hoyer-Larsen -- and suddenly the physical demands caught out the Chinese, who went down clutching his left thigh in agony.
After a short break he managed to resume but was virtually playing on one leg.
Sun, in desperation, hit a series of fine smashes which somehow took him to 10-3, only for cramp to strike once more.
With Chinese team and medical officials watching anxiously, Sun laboured on but Rasmussen swept home to the delight of a sizeable Danish contingent in the crowd.
The Dane, winner of the Japan Open in January, said: "When he was hurt, I did not feel it was won. It was important for me at that stage to remain calm and not to lose my concentration."

Sun's third game problems appeared to breach the consecutive play concept that is an important part of badminton. Cramp is not considered an injury and officals seemed to take a lenient view, allowing him time to recover and don a support bandage.

Rasmussen said: "It's difficult to say whether any rules were broken, but I was angry at all the breaks during the third game. All I wanted to do was concentrate on my game and get the crowd behind me to give me encouragement."

Had Hoyer-Larsen softened up the Chinese on Saturday? "I don't know," said Rasmussen, "but this was the hardest game of my life -- and the longest -- so I would imagine it had the same effect on him."
While Sun, beaten finalist at the All England championships in March, had to settle for silver again, the rest of the day was good news for China.

In the women's singles, Ye Zhaoying kept her title with a hard-fought 12-11 11-8 success over number two seed Gong Zhichao and the women's doubles final went to top seeds Gu Jun and Ge Fei, easy 15-1 15-8 winners over compatriots Tang Yongshu and Qin Yiyuan.
